quote: And `SYSRET`, which lowers it, faults outside Ring 0.
problem: The sentence is offered as support for 'no program can raise the bit itself'. A program in Ring 3 already has the bit low, so the reader cannot see what harm a Ring 3 SYSRET would do, or why guarding the lowering instruction matters, and re-reads.
fix: say what it adds (both directions of the change belong to the kernel, as p1 says) or cut it
reason: Real but small. 'And SYSRET, which lowers it' is attached with 'And' to the claim that no program can raise the bit, yet it is about the other direction. A Ring 3 program is already low, so the reader cannot see why guarding it matters. SYSRET really does #GP when CPL is not 0 (Intel SDM), so the fact is right and only the point of the sentence is missing.
judge_fix: Replace the last sentence with: "And `SYSRET`, the way back down, faults outside Ring 0: the kernel alone moves the bit, in either direction."

quote: using details no real fault produced
problem: The reader was never told that a real fault hands its handler information (which address faulted, what kind of access). So they cannot say why handling a faked int 14 does harm and is not just a harmless check that finds nothing to fix, and the reason DPL exists rests on that.
fix: name the details: a real page fault records the faulting address (and an error code); int 14 supplies neither, so the handler acts on a stale address
reason: 'Using details no real fault produced' is vague, and the reader is never told that a real fault hands the handler anything. Fact check: a real page fault loads the faulting address into CR2 and pushes an error code. `int 14` does neither, because software interrupts push no error code and leave CR2 at the last real fault. The handler would therefore act on a stale address. That is the actual harm, and the reason DPL exists rests on it.
judge_fix: Replace 'using details no real fault produced' with: "acting on the address of some earlier fault, because a real page fault records the address that failed and `int 14` records nothing". The sentence then reads: '...would go to work on a fault that never happened, acting on the address of some earlier fault, because a real page fault records the address that failed and `int 14` records nothing.'

problem: Severity high, the reader stops here. p4 has just said a system call made with SYSCALL skips the IDT, and Fig BR.2 shows it jumping through MSR_LSTAR, but this SOURCE box draws SYSCALL as an IDT source, so the reader has to work out which is true. This is a factual error that §4g has already corrected in the prose; it is open in STATE.md as BLOCKED ON TIGER.
fix: relabel the box 'int 0x80 (legacy)' (owner call, docs/pass-29-owner-calls.md §C)
reason: fig-br-3 is on the kept_original list. The error is real: SYSCALL does not go through the IDT, as chBridge-trap-p4 says, so the SOURCE box 'SYSCALL or int 0x80' contradicts the prose. Only the owner can change a kept-original figure. Recommended owner call: relabel the box 'int 0x80 (legacy)' and leave SYSCALL to Fig BR.2.
judge_fix: Relabel the SOURCE box 'SYSCALL or int 0x80' as 'int 0x80 (legacy)'.

quote: When any trap fires, the CPU reads the IDT base address from its IDTR register
problem: Severity medium-high. The section uses 'trap' to include SYSCALL (p1, p2, p7), and p4 just said SYSCALL skips this table, so 'any trap' contradicts the prose. The closing 'every involuntary entry into the kernel', placed right after listing a system call, adds to the doubt about which entries use the table.
fix: 'When an exception, an interrupt or an int instruction fires' (the recommended owner-call fix)
reason: This is the caption of kept-original fig-br-3. The contradiction is real: 'When any trap fires, the CPU reads the IDT base...' conflicts with p4 (SYSCALL skips the table) and with the section's own use of 'trap' for SYSCALL. 'Every involuntary entry into the kernel' also sits oddly after a system call. Only the owner can edit it.

quote: timer (LAPIC)
problem: Severity low: the reader cannot spot this and will not stop. It is still a factual error. On Linux the local APIC timer uses its own vector (0xEC), not 32, and modern Linux maps legacy IRQ 1 (the keyboard) to vector 0x31, not 33. §4g already corrected the 'timer at vector 32' claim in Fig BR.6, so this figure contradicts the ledger.
fix: drop the vector numbers on the timer and keyboard rows (owner call already logged)
reason: The fact is right, so the finding stands, but the figure is a kept original. In Linux on x86 the local APIC timer uses LOCAL_TIMER_VECTOR 0xEC (arch/x86/include/asm/irq_vectors.h). The legacy ISA IRQs start at IRQ0_VECTOR 0x30, so the keyboard (IRQ 1) is 0x31 = 49, not 33. The 32/33 figures are the old remapped-PIC convention. Only the owner can change the figure.
judge_fix: Owner call: drop the vector numbers on the 'timer (LAPIC)' and 'keyboard (IRQ 1)' rows (show '…' or 'a vector in 32–255'). Source: Linux arch/x86/include/asm/irq_vectors.h.

quote: an entry for every page a process could address would take 512 GiB
problem: The reader cannot rebuild 512 GiB. The book never says how much a process can address (48 bits, so 2^36 pages) or how big an entry is (8 bytes). Chapter 1's 'seemingly gigabytes long' (ch1-memory-p8) works out to a table of a few megabytes, so the number reads as a contradiction, and 4 × 9 + 12 = 48 bits on a 64-bit machine is left unexplained too.
fix: give the reachable range (2^48 bytes = 2^36 pages, 8-byte entries), or simply 'more than the RAM itself'
reason: The arithmetic is right (48-bit addresses, 2^36 pages, 8-byte entries, so 2^39 B = 512 GiB). But the number is the justification for the whole four-level design and the page gives none of its inputs. It sets no address width, no entry size and no reach. Ch1 only says 'seemingly gigabytes long', which anchors the reader on a table of a few MB. The 512-entries-per-page and 9+9+9+9+12 facts that follow are what make the number derivable.
judge_fix: Replace 'One flat table with an entry for every page a process could address would take 512 GiB.' with: "Addresses on x86-64 are 48 bits, so a process could address 2^36 pages, and a flat table with an 8-byte entry for each would take 512 GiB."

quote: to stop nearly all of them on a core with a single task
problem: p1 says a stuck program can only be taken back by the tick, and p5 says even killing a misbehaving program depends on it. So the reader cannot work out what happens when the one task on a core that has lost almost all its ticks gets stuck: can the kernel still take it back or kill it? The sentence that follows only answers the sharing question.
fix: one clause saying the few ticks left still let the kernel in, so a stuck lone task can be stopped
reason: A real gap against the section's own thesis. The strip says the tick is the only way back and p5 says even killing a program depends on it. The figure shows a stuck process C. 'Nearly all' hints that some ticks remain but never says so, and the next sentence only covers sharing. Fact: Linux nohz_full keeps a residual slow tick on such a core (Documentation/timers/no_hz.rst), so the kernel can still get in.
judge_fix: Change to: "...to stop nearly all of them on a core with a single task (a slow trickle remains, so the kernel can still take back a stuck task)." Keep the next sentence as is.

quote: Then it makes one MMIO write, to a register called the doorbell
problem: The abbreviation MMIO appears here (and again in 'MMIO loads') but is never introduced: p2 names memory-mapped I/O with no '(MMIO)', so the reader has to stop and work out what MMIO stands for. The heading 'DMA: when the device copies on its own' and p4's 'MMIO write' and 'MMIO loads' then use them. The book's convention is to bracket the expansion at first use, and p2 does exactly that for 'interrupt request (IRQ)'. quote: When any trap fires, the CPU reads the IDT base address from its IDTR register
problem: The section calls system calls traps ('System calls are not the only traps'), and p4 says SYSCALL skips the IDT. quote: Then one instruction (SYSRET on x86-64, ERET on ARM) switches the CPU to Ring 3
problem: Linux does not enter the first user program with SYSRET. ret_from_fork_asm jumps to swapgs_restore_regs_and_return_to_usermode, which ends in IRETQ (ERETU on FRED machines). SYSRET is the fast return from a SYSCALL. The mechanism is right (one privileged return instruction drops to Ring 3); only the named instruction is wrong for x86-64 Linux. p8's 'SYSRET ... faults outside Ring 0' stays true.
fix: 'Then one instruction (IRET or SYSRET on x86-64, ERET on ARM) switches the CPU to Ring 3 ...'. Source: linux arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S (ret_from_fork_asm → swapgs_restore_regs_and_return_to_usermode → iretq).
reason: Linux x86-64 enters the first user program via ret_from_fork_asm -> swapgs_restore_regs_and_return_to_usermode, which ends in IRETQ; SYSRET is the fast return from SYSCALL. The mechanism in p6 is right but the named instruction is not what a kernel does here. Low severity, two-word fix, p8's SYSRET claim stays true.
judge_fix: chBridge-mode-p6: 'Then one instruction (`IRET` or `SYSRET` on x86-64, `ERET` on ARM) switches the CPU to Ring 3 and jumps to the start of the first user program.' Source: linux arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S (ret_from_fork_asm).

quote: Then a store to the next page up, 0x7fff_a3c5_0010
problem: Arithmetic. With 4 KiB pages the page number is everything above the last three hex digits, so 0x7fff_a3c5_0010 is 0x10000 bytes above 0x7fff_a3c4_0010: 16 pages up, not the next page (that would be 0x7fff_a3c4_1010). The §4g row's point stands (the store goes to a different page, so it misses the TLB); only 'next' is wrong. The same shorthand puts Fig BR.5's 'page a3c?' labels one hex digit off the real page numbers (0x7fffa3c40, ...).
fix: Smallest fix, in the desc: 'Then a store to another page, 0x7fff_a3c5_0010: ...'. Fuller fix that makes 'next page' and BR.5's labels exact: use 0x7fff_fa3c_4010 and 0x7fff_fa3c_5010 (page numbers ending a3c4, a3c5) with physical 0xa20_0010 (frame a200, offset 0x010 unchanged).
reason: Arithmetic holds: with 4 KiB pages 0x7fff_a3c5_0010 is 16 pages above 0x7fff_a3c4_0010. Only the hidden <desc> says 'next page up'; the drawn labels do not, so it is low severity, but screen-reader text states a false fact and the fix is one phrase. BR.5's 'page a3c? (last digit shown)' is an explicit abbreviation and can stay.
judge_fix: Fig BR.4 <desc>: 'Then a store to another page, 0x7fff_a3c5_0010: it misses the TLB too, ...' (replace 'the next page up'). Also fix the §4g row 615 wording 'next page up' to 'another page'.

quote: network card | from 0xC010_0000 | GPU frame buffer | from 0xC000_0000
problem: A map billed as 'typical' leaves the GPU frame buffer only 0xC000_0000 to 0xC00F_FFFF, which is 1 MiB. One 1920×1080 screen at 4 bytes a pixel needs about 7.9 MiB, and GPU frame-buffer apertures are typically 256 MiB or more. 'Not to scale' covers the drawn heights, not the printed addresses, which fix the sizes.
fix: Move the network card to 'from 0xD000_0000' and its store to 'store x at 0xD000_0018', which leaves the frame buffer a 256 MiB window. Keep the frame buffer store at 0xC000_0400.
reason: With the network card at 0xC010_0000 the frame buffer window is exactly 1 MiB, less than one 1080p frame (about 7.9 MiB), while the strip says the addresses are typical. Real window sizes are 256 MiB or more. Equal-length text, so no layout risk.
judge_fix: Fig BR.7: network card 'from 0xD000_0000' and its store 'store x at 0xD000_0018' (in the drawn label, the animated store text and the <desc>/words list); GPU frame buffer stays 'from 0xC000_0000', store at 0xC000_0400. Also update docs/pass-30-gate2-record.md label list.

quote: (Linux's NO_HZ_IDLE and NO_HZ_FULL), saving power.
problem: The strip gives both options the purpose of saving power. NO_HZ_IDLE saves power; NO_HZ_FULL exists for real-time latency and HPC throughput, and kernel docs list extra costs for it (dearer user/kernel transitions), not energy savings. chBridge-timer-p4 already states this correctly, so the strip contradicts the prose beside it.
fix: 'Tickless. An idle core can skip ticks entirely to save power (Linux's NO_HZ_IDLE), and for real-time and HPC work a core running one task can almost stop them (NO_HZ_FULL).' Source: docs.kernel.org/timers/no_hz.html.
reason: The strip gives both NO_HZ_IDLE and NO_HZ_FULL the purpose 'saving power'. NO_HZ_FULL exists for real-time and HPC jitter (docs.kernel.org/timers/no_hz.html), which chBridge-timer-p4 states correctly. The strip contradicts the prose beside it.
judge_fix: Strip bullet: '*Tickless.* An idle core can skip ticks entirely to save power (Linux's NO_HZ_IDLE), and for real-time and high-performance work a core running one task can almost stop them (NO_HZ_FULL).'

quote: The instruction does not run and no error code comes back
problem: #GP is one of the x86 exceptions that does push an error code (0 for a privileged-instruction violation) onto the kernel handler's stack. The intended meaning is that nothing returns to the program, but the literal reading is wrong, and a reader who knows x86 will stop on it.
fix: 'The instruction does not run and nothing returns to the program; the CPU jumps to the handler ...'. Source: Intel SDM vol. 3A, 'Interrupt 13, General Protection Exception (#GP)': error code yes, 0 here.
reason: #GP pushes an error code (0 for a privileged-instruction violation) on the handler's stack, so the literal sentence is false for x86 even though the intent is that nothing returns to the program. Cheap, unambiguous fix; an x86-literate reader would stop on it.
judge_fix: Fig BR.1 strip, #GP bullet: 'A general-protection fault. The instruction does not run and nothing returns to the program; the CPU jumps to the handler the kernel set up, and the kernel decides what happens to the program.' Source: Intel SDM vol. 3A, Interrupt 13 (#GP).

quote: under every forced switch from one process to another, a timer tick that took the CPU back
problem: 'Every' overclaims. A forced switch also happens when a device interrupt wakes a task the scheduler prefers: a keyboard or disk interrupt wakes an interactive process and the kernel preempts the running one on the way out of that interrupt, with no tick involved. §4g settled who takes the CPU back (the tick, not a timer calling schedule()). The universal 'every' is a separate issue.
fix: 'under every forced switch from one process to another, an interrupt, most often a timer tick, that took the CPU back; ...'. Source: Linux kernel/sched/fair.c wakeup preemption (resched_curr on wakeup).
reason: 'Every forced switch ... a timer tick' overclaims: Linux also preempts on return from a device interrupt that wakes a preferred task (wakeup preemption in kernel/sched/fair.c). The ledger fix (tick, not a timer calling schedule()) stays intact. Two independent readers (13 and 28) hit it.
judge_fix: chBridge-synthesis-p6: 'under every time-slice switch from one process to another, a timer tick that took the CPU back; under the `read()` system call, ...' (replace 'every forced switch').

problem: chBridge-mode-p6: 'one instruction (SYSRET on x86-64 ...) switches the CPU to Ring 3 and jumps to the start of the first user program'. Linux x86-64 enters its first user process through the IRET path: ret_from_fork_asm ends in swapgs_restore_regs_and_return_to_usermode, which runs IRETQ. SYSRET is the fast return from a system call. Also, ARM's ERET goes to EL0, and ARM has exception levels, not rings, so 'Ring 3' is loose for ARM. Suggest 'SYSRET or IRET'.
reason: Duplicate of 6: Linux x86-64 enters the first user program through the IRET path. The ARM 'Ring 3 is loose' remark is not a defect: the book uses Ring 3 as its name for user mode throughout.
judge_fix: Same as 6: '(`IRET` or `SYSRET` on x86-64, `ERET` on ARM)'. No change for 'Ring 3'.

problem: fig-br-1 How it works, #GP: 'no error code comes back'. #GP does push an error code (often 0) for the kernel's handler. The phrase means the program gets nothing back, as the old caption made clear, but it can read as a claim about the hardware. Low.
reason: Duplicate of 12: 'no error code comes back' is false as a hardware statement (#GP pushes error code 0).
judge_fix: Same as 12: 'The instruction does not run and nothing returns to the program; the CPU jumps to the handler the kernel set up, ...'.

problem: Fig BR.4 picture description: 'a store to the next page up, 0x7fff_a3c5_0010'. With 4 KiB pages the offset is the last three hex digits, so 0x7fff_a3c4_0010 is on page 0x7_fffa_3c40, and 0x7fff_a3c5_0010 is 0x10000 bytes (64 KiB, 16 pages) higher. The next page up would be 0x7fff_a3c4_1010. Fig BR.5's labels 'a3c4 -> a200' and 'a3c5 -> b731' reuse BR.4's four-digit underscore groups as if they were page numbers, but those digits are address bits 16 to 31, not the page number. A reader who checks against 'last twelve bits = offset' finds the two figures disagree.
reason: Duplicate of 7: the arithmetic point is right, but only in the hidden <desc>. BR.5's four-digit labels are an explicit abbreviation ('last digit shown') and need no change.
judge_fix: Same as 7: '<desc> ... Then a store to another page, 0x7fff_a3c5_0010: ...'.

problem: Fig BR.7 (low): the GPU frame buffer starts at 0xC000_0000 and the network card's registers at 0xC010_0000. That leaves the frame buffer only 1 MiB. A 1920x1080 screen at 4 bytes a pixel needs about 8 MB, and GPU frame-buffer windows are usually 256 MiB or more. So for this pair, the strip's claim 'the addresses shown are typical' does not hold. A gap such as the network card at 0xD000_0000 would be realistic.
reason: Duplicate of 9 (frame buffer window of 1 MiB against a claim of typical addresses).
judge_fix: Same as 9: network card at 0xD000_0000, store at 0xD000_0018.

problem: chBridge-synthesis-p6 (severity low): 'under every forced switch from one process to another, a timer tick that took the CPU back' is too strong. In Linux an involuntary switch also happens on return from a device interrupt that woke a higher-priority task, or from a reschedule inter-processor interrupt, with no tick involved. Fig BR.8 in this Part already shows an IRQ waking process A. The timer guarantees the kernel a turn; it is not under every forced switch. reason: Duplicate of 13: 'every forced switch' overclaims (wakeup preemption after a device interrupt).

quote: No program can raise the bit itself: a trap raises it
problem: p2 and Fig BR.1 say kernel mode is CPL 00 and user mode is 11. Read literally, 'raise the bit' to enter the kernel and 'SYSRET, which lowers it' are the wrong way round, so a reader comparing with the figure stops. The rest of the sentence ('keeps in registers and S pages that Ring 3 cannot change') is hard to parse and makes in advance the point that trap-p7's strip makes in full.

And `SYSRET`, which returns the CPU to Ring 3, faults outside Ring 0." (SYSRET is privileged and raises #GP when CPL is not 0.)

quote: the device then copies it into RAM on its own while the CPU runs something else

quote: The instruction does not run and no error code comes back
problem: On x86 a #GP does push an error code for the handler (0 for a privilege violation). The strip means that the program gets no result, but it says the opposite of the SDM in x86's own vocabulary.

reason: A #GP does push an error code to the handler (0 for a privilege violation), per the Intel SDM, so 'no error code comes back' is false in x86's own vocabulary. For a program 'comes back' is vague as well. The strip is not owner text. The sentence is wrong and the fix is a few words.
judge_fix: '*#GP.* A general-protection fault. The instruction does not run and the program gets no result; the CPU jumps to the handler the kernel set up, and the kernel decides what happens to the program.'
